note: Authored lane_check.py in full (344 lines) from a rule-by-rule contract, writing it straight to disk. Structure, API and every one of the ten stated rules came back correct on the first pass, including the entity-wise tautology matcher and the deliberate under-match guard on an unknown change set. Two omissions the gate supplied: the module docstring the contract asked for was absent, and the file carried no shebang.

Blind cross-family refutation, and by some distance the most valuable review of this wave. Six findings were real and all six are fixed: (1) `git status --porcelain` collapses an untracked DIRECTORY to 'newdir/', which matches no file glob, so a scoped check silently skipped on exactly the change it was written for — MEASURED true before curing; (2) `pytest x || true` is a real check whose failure is swallowed, and an all()-over-entities tautology rule let it through as PASS — the reward-hacking shape the rule exists to refuse, dressed as a real check; (3) one anti-loop marker shared between two block reasons meant a lane-check block CONSUMED the pre-existing dirty guard's only shot, so adding a feature silently un-armed a protection already in force; (4) a path containing a space arrives quoted from both git commands and matches nothing — MEASURED; (5) the ABSENT innocence promise was FALSE at the wiring, because the change set was evaluated as a function argument, so three git subprocesses ran on every termination fleet-wide with no contract present, and the library's own tests were structurally blind to it; (6) shell=True on a contract file is a zero-click RCE when a subagent clones an external repository to read it — the trust-boundary argument was true of our worktrees and false of a clone. Two MINORs also accepted (a root-directory path check that bricked on '/', a 900s timeout ceiling unreasonable for a synchronous stop hook). Its tone was hostile and its substance was right.
Out of credits across the whole Codex seat, re-confirmed. Would have been the natural second reviewer here.
